style_prompt: Convert this image into an unmistakable Pixar-style 3D animated cartoon frame. The ENTIRE scene — people, clothing, props, and background — must look like a still from a high-end 3D animated feature film, never like a photograph or a lightly filtered photo: stylized cartoon rendering throughout, soft cinematic lighting, rich saturated colors, gently rounded simplified forms, smooth stylized cartoon skin with no photorealistic skin texture or pores, simplified painterly backgrounds, and expressive animation-studio shading. LIKENESS IS CRITICAL: the people must remain instantly recognizable as the same real individuals, as if this exact family were cast as characters in a Pixar-style film about themselves. Preserve each person's true facial structure and proportions: face shape, jawline, chin, nose size and shape, REAL eye size and spacing (do not enlarge the eyes), eyebrow shape and thickness, lip shape, their actual hairstyle, hairline and hair color, skin tone, age, and body type, plus distinctive features (freckles, moles, glasses, facial hair). Stylize the rendering, not the person: do not slim faces, smooth away distinguishing features, or beautify anyone into a generic cartoon character. HAIR IS NEVER RESTORED OR IMPROVED. Copy each person's hair exactly as the photo shows it — INCLUDING THE ABSENCE OF IT. A shaved or bald head stays completely bald: do NOT add a fringe, stubble, or a band of hair around the ears, sides or back, and never lower a receding hairline. This is the most common way these portraits go wrong — a real styling gave a cleanly bald man dark hair around his ears. It cuts both ways: do not thicken thinning hair, lengthen short hair, straighten curls, or shift its colour. EYEWEAR IS AN IDENTIFYING FEATURE, not an accessory to reinterpret: keep the exact frame shape, size and colour and the exact lens tint. Wraparound mirrored sport sunglasses must not become square white-framed ones. PEOPLE FIRST — THE SUBJECTS ARE THE PICTURE. Spend the detail where the faces are. When several people share the frame, render EACH face with the care of a solo portrait and keep them clearly distinct individuals; never let them drift toward one shared generic cartoon face. The background — walls, stonework, stacked wood, foliage, furniture, distant scenery — is context, not subject: keep its colours, layout and mood recognisable but simplify it freely. An approximate background with exact faces is a SUCCESS; a beautifully detailed background with generic faces is a FAILURE. If detail must be lost somewhere, lose it in the background — never in a face, a hairline, the shape and colour of someone's glasses, or a distinguishing feature. FRAMING — NEVER CUT A PERSON OFF. Every person in the photo must sit COMPLETELY inside the 16:9 frame from the top of their hair down, with a clear band of background above the tallest head. Never crop through a head, hair, face or shoulders, and never let anyone touch the top edge. This rule OUTRANKS every other framing instruction below: a sliced-off head is the worst failure this step can produce, and it is the one that keeps happening — a vertical photo of a couple on a salt flat came back with the man's scalp cut away at the top edge. A TALL (PORTRAIT) SOURCE IS THE DANGEROUS CASE, because height has to go somewhere to make a wide frame: take it off the BOTTOM — feet, legs, foreground ground — and off empty sky at the top only down to that band of headroom; NEVER off the heads. If the people still do not fit, pull the camera BACK and render them a little smaller: smaller people are an acceptable outcome, a cropped head is not. Where nobody is at risk of being cut, keep the people at least as large in the frame as they are in the source photo, and crop INTO the scene rather than inventing extra scenery at the sides — losing the edges of a wall or the top of a building is fine, shrinking the people to make room for more background is not. If the SOURCE photo itself already cuts someone off, keep that framing exactly — this rule is about never introducing a NEW crop, never about inventing the missing part of a person. Preserve the camera angle, the subjects' placement relative to each other, their clothing, and the scene's content. Output in 16:9.
scratch_style_prompt: Create Pixar-style 3D animated cartoon visuals — every frame must look like a still from a high-end 3D animated feature film, never photorealistic: soft cinematic lighting, expressive character design, clean rounded shapes, rich saturated colors, smooth stylized cartoon skin, simplified painterly backgrounds, and high-quality animation-studio rendering. Keep the visual identity consistent across all frames. Frame every character completely inside the shot with a clear band of background above the tallest head — never crop a head, face or hair at the top edge; pull the camera back instead.
motion_prompt: Natural, continuous in-scene motion connecting the start frame to the end frame: the characters and environment move and evolve believably, with camera movement only as needed to follow the action. Preserve each person's identity, environment, colors, and composition. If the people in the two frames are different individuals, the first person exits the frame or passes behind something while the other enters or is revealed — never transform or morph one person into another. If the same people appear in both frames but in different positions, each person physically moves to their new position — never swap or blend one person into another in place. No sudden cuts, no text, no distortion, no camera shake. The final frame should closely match the provided end image.
fal_negative_prompt: blurry, low quality, distorted face, warped features, morphing, extra limbs, extra fingers, flickering, jittery movement, text overlay, subtitles, captions, watermark, sudden cuts
default_sfx_prompt: Ambient sound and natural sound effects matching the on-screen action. No music, no speech, no narration.
